title: Efficient Centrality Maximization with Rademacher Averages

problem.claim: Identify the k most central nodes of a graph for network-analysis applications.

gap.claim: Exact centrality computation does not scale to modern-sized networks, creating a need for rigorous and efficiently computable randomized approximations.

contributions.claim: CentRA uses progressive sampling to compute high-quality approximations of the set of k most central nodes.
CentRA efficiently estimates Monte Carlo Rademacher Averages to obtain sharp data-dependent approximation bounds.
The work analyzes sample complexity using VC-dimension and derives bounds that scale with graph vertex diameter and the centrality of interest.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe CentRA as the first progressive-sampling algorithm for computing high-quality approximations of the k most central nodes and describe its Rademacher-Average estimation approach as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the bounds significantly improve on looser bounds from standard techniques.
On large real-world networks, the authors report that CentRA significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art approximation algorithm in number of samples, running time, and accuracy.

narrative_sequence.summary: Centrality maximization seeks the k most central graph nodes and supports network-analysis applications.
Exact centrality computation does not scale, motivating randomized approximations.
CentRA applies progressive sampling and efficient Monte Carlo Rademacher-Average estimation.
The work studies sample complexity using VC-dimension and graph- and centrality-dependent characteristics.
The authors apply CentRA to large real-world networks and report improvements over a state-of-the-art approximation algorithm.

source_observation.claim: Approximation bounds can be tightened by incorporating graph-specific and centrality-specific characteristics.

interpretation.claim: Data-dependent complexity analysis may yield more efficient sampling requirements than generic bounds.

application.claim: For scalable graph algorithms, consider progressive sampling with complexity bounds adapted to structural properties of the graph and target measure.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether these advantages hold beyond the evaluated networks and centrality settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the centrality measures evaluated.
The abstract does not provide quantitative sample, runtime, or accuracy results.
The abstract does not describe experimental datasets or implementation details.
